sources.title: TodoMVC behavior reference: precise functional contract

model.vision: A dependable todo list a small team can use to capture, finish, and clear away their work.

objectives.statement: A small team can start using the todo list the day after delivery, with no training, setup, or migration effort.
No recorded todo is ever lost: every todo, with its wording and done state, is still present when the user returns after closing the app or restarting their device.
Capturing and correcting work is low-friction: a user records, rewords, or removes a todo in a single step, never by deleting and re-entering it.
Users always know where they stand: the number of todos still left to do is visible at a glance, and users can review all, remaining, or finished work as they prefer.
Finished work gets out of the way: users can mark todos done one at a time or all at once (and reverse either), and sweep away everything already finished in one action.
The team's automated assistants and other hosted tools can work the same todo list a person works, so the list fits into how the team already operates rather than standing apart from it.

model.mission: Reproduce the familiar reference todo experience faithfully and nothing beyond it, keep every list safely on the team's behalf rather than on the user's device, and offer every list action identically to people and to the team's automated assistants.

items.definition: The small group of people who share and work one todo list as part of how they already operate.
A person on the team who captures, rewords, finishes, removes, and reviews todos on the list.
One of the team's software helpers or hosted tools that works the same todo list, performing every list action a team member can.
One piece of work the team wants to remember, made up of its wording (title) and whether it is done.
The free-text wording of a todo that says what the work is; it must contain more than blank space.
Whether a todo is finished (done) or still left to do (remaining); every new todo starts as remaining.
A todo that is not yet done (shown under the Active view).
A todo that has been marked done (shown under the Completed view).
Add a new remaining todo with the given title to the end of the list; blank wording captures nothing.
Change an existing todo's title in place, without removing and re-capturing it; rewording to blank removes the todo instead.
Back out of a reword in progress so the todo keeps its original title unchanged.
Take a single todo off the list, whatever its done state, leaving every other todo untouched.
Flip one todo between done and remaining without affecting any other todo.
In one action, make every todo done; if every todo is already done, the same action makes every todo remaining again.
In one action, take every finished todo off the list, leaving remaining todos untouched; does nothing when nothing is finished.
Look at the list through a chosen view (All, Active, or Completed) without changing any todo.
The always-visible number of todos still left to do ('items left'), counted over the whole list regardless of the view in use.
Hold every todo, with its title and done state, on the team's behalf so it is still there when a user returns after closing the app or restarting their device.
A way of looking at the list: All (every todo), Active (remaining todos only), or Completed (finished todos only); the current view is always visibly indicated.
Deciding whether proposed wording is meaningful (not empty or blank) before a todo is captured or reworded.
Deciding what Mark All Done does: make all remaining when every todo is already done, otherwise make all done (including when the list is mixed).
Choosing which todos belong in the current view by their done state, never altering the todos themselves.
Counting the todos that are not done across the whole list, refreshed after every action that changes which todos remain.
Store a newly captured todo at the end of the team's kept list.
Read back the team's kept list of todos, in order, with each title and done state.
Store a changed title or done state for one or more kept todos.
Erase one kept todo, or every kept todo that is finished, from the team's list.
The ordered collection of the team's todos that the system keeps on their behalf, away from any one user's device, so it survives closing the app, device restarts, and service restarts.

model.rationale: recommend DecompressedSolution: lowest in-band composite risk (0.325) at 140.0 days (App C risk-crossover exclusions applied)

items.name: Presentation-host volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: where and inside what the list is shown to a Team Member, and how they act on it. Today there are already two hosts: a standalone web app in a browser and an MCP Apps surface embedded in whatever MCP host the team uses ('embedded the same way our other MCP-hosted UIs are'). Each host has its own rendering limits, gestures (double-click or Enter or Escape editing versus host-mediated actions), styling, and lifecycle. WHY volatile: different team members reach the same list through different hosts at the same moment, and embedding hosts are new and multiplying. LIKELIHOOD: high. The MCP Apps embedding model is less than two years old and host capabilities change every few months. Over a multi-year life the team will add or swap at least one host, and likely several. EFFECT if not encapsulated: list rules (Title Check, Aggregate Done Decision, View Selection, Remaining Tally) would be copied into each host's UI code, and every new host would re-implement them and drift from the reference experience the mission requires to be reproduced faithfully. Longevity grounding: the founder brief names two hosts on day one, and embedding hosts change several times a year, well inside the system's lifespan. Traces are empty only because the Required Behaviors are not yet committed on this branch. Source: founder brief, delivery paragraph (web app plus MCP Apps surface).

items.name: Invocation-protocol volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the wire protocol through which callers (people's clients and the team's Automated Assistants) invoke list actions. Today these are an ordinary web API and an MCP surface, and the mission says both must offer every action identically. WHY volatile: agent-tool protocols are the fastest-moving part of this team's stack. The MCP specification has had several revisions since 2024 (transport, auth, tool-schema changes), and the team says it builds 'everything else here' this way, so it will follow those revisions. LIKELIHOOD: near-certain. At least one breaking revision per year of the MCP surface, and plausibly a further protocol for new agent tooling. EFFECT if not encapsulated: list actions written against one protocol would have to be rewritten or duplicated for each protocol, and people and assistants would drift apart, breaking the mission's 'identically to people and to the team's automated assistants'. Longevity grounding: the protocol revision rate (several per year) falls well inside the system's lifespan. Traces are empty only because the Required Behaviors are not yet committed on this branch. Source: founder brief ('reachable both as an ordinary web API and as an MCP surface'), mission objective 6.

items.name: Storage volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the technology and location in which the Todo List is kept so that it survives closing the app, device restarts, and service restarts (Keep List: Record Todo, Retrieve List, Revise Todo, Discard Todos). WHY volatile: a trial deployment 'a small team could start using tomorrow' will start on the simplest durable store. If the trial succeeds, the store will move to whatever the team's standard managed store is, and its durability, backup, and hosting will change with it. LIKELIHOOD: high. Moving storage technology after a successful trial is the most common change in small internal services, typically within the first one to two years. EFFECT if not encapsulated: storage specifics (queries, transactions, ordering by insertion, bulk clear of finished todos) would leak into every list action and into both invocation surfaces. A store migration would then touch the whole system and put at risk the mission's 'No recorded todo is ever lost'. Longevity grounding: storage technology for internal services is typically replaced on a one-to-three-year cycle, inside the system's lifespan. Traces are empty only because the Required Behaviors are not yet committed on this branch. Source: behavior contract §9 (persistence backed by the real backend service), mission objective 2.

items.name: Caller-identity volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: how the system establishes who is calling, whether a Team Member through some host or an Automated Assistant through some tool, and so which kept list the call acts on. WHY volatile: the list is kept on the caller's behalf, away from any device, so a device can no longer stand in for identity. People and assistants identify themselves in very different ways (browser session, MCP host-delegated auth, service credentials for hosted tools), and each new host or assistant brings its own scheme. The sources also differ on ownership: the contract says one user's list, while the approved glossary says the team works one list. That difference is itself evidence that how a caller is resolved to a list varies. LIKELIHOOD: high. Every new presentation host or assistant integration (see the two entries above) brings an identity scheme, and the team's identity provider itself will change over a multi-year life. EFFECT if not encapsulated: identity checks and caller-to-list resolution would spread through every action and protocol handler. Adding an assistant or changing how lists are owned would then ripple through the whole system. This entry does NOT bring in multi-user sharing, which stays out of scope (see rejected). It insulates only how a caller is resolved to the list it may act on. Longevity grounding: identity schemes for agent tooling have changed several times since 2024 (MCP auth revisions), inside the system's lifespan. Traces are empty only because the Required Behaviors are not yet committed on this branch. Source: mission ('keep every list safely on the team's behalf rather than on the user's device', 'identically to people and to the team's automated assistants'), glossary Automated Assistant and Keep List.

items.name: Change-propagation volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: how a change one actor makes to a list reaches another actor's open view of the same list. Examples are an Automated Assistant capturing or clearing todos while a Team Member has the web app or an embedded surface open. Possible mechanisms include re-reading after each action, polling, server push, and host-delivered notifications. WHY volatile: the mission makes people and assistants co-workers on the same list, and the contract requires the Remaining Count to always be the true count, refreshed after every changing action. With more than one actor, 'after every action' must include actions taken elsewhere. Which mechanism works depends on the host and protocol, and it changes as assistants take on more of the work. LIKELIHOOD: medium-high. The first assistant integration exposes stale views, and the team's growing use of agent tooling ('so our other agent tooling can drive it too') keeps raising how often others make changes. EFFECT if not encapsulated: each client would build its own refresh logic tied to one protocol. Stale counts and views would break mission objective 4 ('users always know where they stand'), and changing the mechanism would mean editing every client. Likely an operational-concept disposition (pub/sub) rather than its own component. Longevity grounding: the team's agent tooling is growing now, so the rate of changes made by someone else rises over the lifespan. Traces are empty only because the Required Behaviors are not yet committed on this branch. Source: behavior contract §8, mission objectives 4 and 6.

rejected.name: List-sharing volatility (one list worked by several people)
rejected.reason: The behavior contract lists 'multi-user sharing' as out of scope and says it 'must not be assumed required', and the PM's glossary critique flagged exactly this. Designing for shared multi-user lists would design for a business the requirements explicitly exclude. Whatever stays real (which list a caller is resolved to) is covered by Caller-identity volatility.

rejected.name: Todo-shape volatility (due dates, priorities, tags/categories)
rejected.reason: All three are named out of scope by the contract, and the mission says to reproduce the reference experience 'and nothing beyond it'. Adding a field to a two-field record is ordinary data change, not a ripple-causing volatility.

rejected.name: Title-check rules volatility
rejected.reason: The only rule is 'not empty or whitespace-only'. Changing it is a single conditional inside the list rules, with no structural impact.

rejected.name: Aggregate-done (toggle-all) rule volatility
rejected.reason: The all-done-then-all-remaining toggle is the fixed TodoMVC reference behavior that 'many frontend example apps implement identically'. It changes only if the reference itself changes.

rejected.name: View-filter set volatility (All/Active/Completed)
rejected.reason: The three views are fixed by the reference contract and are the same across every TodoMVC implementation. Each view is just a filter on done state, so even adding one would be a conditional.

rejected.name: Remaining-count calculation volatility
rejected.reason: Counting todos that are not done across the whole list is a single computation with no realistic alternative. Keeping it fresh across actors is covered by Change-propagation volatility.

rejected.name: List-operation set volatility (capture, reword, remove, mark, clear)
rejected.reason: The operations are the fixed TodoMVC contract and the mission requires reproducing them faithfully and nothing beyond. Every competing todo app offers this same core.

rejected.name: Ordering volatility (drag-to-reorder, sort orders)
rejected.reason: The contract fixes append-to-end order and names drag-to-reorder out of scope. No source suggests other orderings.

rejected.name: Undo/redo history volatility
rejected.reason: Explicitly out of scope in the contract. Reversing Mark Todo Done and Mark All Done is already a toggle, not a history.

rejected.name: Offline-sync volatility
rejected.reason: Explicitly out of scope. The mission moves the list off the device to the service, the opposite of offline-first.

rejected.name: Edit-gesture volatility (double-click, Enter, blur, Escape)
rejected.reason: How a reword is started, committed, or abandoned depends on the host. It is the same underlying change as Presentation-host volatility.

rejected.name: Look-and-feel / host-theming volatility
rejected.reason: Matching the styling of the embedding MCP host is part of what differs per presentation host. Folded into Presentation-host volatility.

rejected.name: MCP specification revision volatility
rejected.reason: A specific case of the wire protocol changing. Folded into Invocation-protocol volatility.

rejected.name: Assistant-tooling vendor volatility (which agent tools drive the list)
rejected.reason: New assistant tools reach the list through some invocation protocol and identify themselves through some identity scheme. Folded into Invocation-protocol volatility and Caller-identity volatility.

rejected.name: Durability-guarantee volatility (surviving service restarts, backups)
rejected.reason: How durable the kept list is depends on the chosen store and how it is hosted. Folded into Storage volatility.

rejected.name: Assistant permission volatility (assistants allowed fewer actions than people)
rejected.reason: The mission requires every list action to be offered identically to people and assistants. A per-actor permission split contradicts the mission and has no source. Telling actors apart is covered by Caller-identity volatility.

rejected.name: Deployment-venue volatility (where the service is hosted)
rejected.reason: 'Built the way we build everything else here' fixes one house deployment style. Where the service runs is a configuration and operational-concept choice, not a change that ripples through the decomposition. Store hosting is covered by Storage volatility.

rejected.name: Scale volatility (many teams, very large lists)
rejected.reason: The brief is a trial for 'a small team'. No source suggests growth to many teams or large lists, so designing for it would be designing for a hypothetical business.

rejected.name: Finished-todo retention volatility (archive instead of erase on Clear Finished)
rejected.reason: The contract says Clear Finished removes finished todos. No source asks for archives or history, and undo/history is out of scope.

rejected.name: Remaining-count wording / localization volatility
rejected.reason: The 'items left' text and its plural forms are presentation strings handled by a formatter.

rejected.name: Logging / reporting block
rejected.reason: A habitual siren-song block (ch. 2 §3.6). No source asks for reporting or analytics on todos, so there is no business volatility behind it.

rejected.name: View-selection persistence volatility (remembering or linking the chosen view)
rejected.reason: Whether the current view is kept in a URL or session is a host-local presentation detail. It is handled per host and does not touch the list rules or storage.

decisions.essenceRationale: Changing the team's kept list is what every customer of this system buys: whoever the caller is (a Team Member through any host, or an Automated Assistant through any protocol) and whichever reference action they invoke, the same flow applies: resolve the caller to their list, check the wording, apply the fixed TodoMVC list rules against the current list, keep the result durably on the team's behalf, and make the change visible to everyone else working the list. The six customer-named actions (capture, reword, remove, mark done, mark all done, clear finished) are permutations of this one abstraction that differ only in which rule applies. The abstraction is nearly immutable because the reference contract fixes the rules, while hosts, protocols, stores, and identity schemes change around it. It is also what sets the product apart from the many browser-only TodoMVC demos: the same rule-governed change, offered identically to people and assistants and never lost. It crosses every committed volatility seam: Presentation-host and Invocation-protocol (any caller, any surface), Caller-identity (resolve the caller to a list), Storage (keep the change), and Change-propagation (tell other open views).

nodes.label: Team Member or Automated Assistant opens the list or chooses a view (All, Active, Completed)
Resolve the caller to the kept list it may look at
Caller resolved to a list?
Caller is told the request was not accepted
Retrieve the kept list's todos in order, with each title and done state
Select the todos belonging to the chosen view and tally the remaining todos across the whole list
Caller sees the chosen view (visibly indicated) and the items-left count; no todo changes
Re-run whenever an open view is told the list changed elsewhere (Work the Kept List), so the view and count stay true

decisions.essenceRationale: Knowing where you stand is the other half of what every customer gets from the list (mission objective 4): at any moment, from any host or assistant, the caller sees the kept list through a chosen view together with the true items-left count over the whole list, and nothing on the list changes because they looked. Choosing a view, reading the counter, coming back after closing the tab or restarting a laptop, and looking at the list embedded in an MCP host are all permutations of this one read-only abstraction, which needs a name of its own because customers only ever describe its pieces. It is nearly immutable: the three views and the count are fixed by the reference contract. It differentiates the product because the list it reads is kept on the team's behalf, so it is still there on return and is the same list an assistant just changed, unlike a device-local demo. It crosses the Presentation-host, Invocation-protocol, Caller-identity, and Storage seams, and it is the receiving end of Change-propagation (it re-runs when an open view is told the list changed).

components.name: WebApp
components.encapsulates: Encapsulates Presentation-host volatility for the browser host. Web app for Team Members; routes to KeptListManager.

components.name: McpAppsSurface
components.encapsulates: Encapsulates Presentation-host volatility for embedding MCP hosts. Team Members work the list; routes to KeptListManager.

components.name: ListApi
components.encapsulates: Encapsulates Invocation-protocol volatility for the web API. Routes every list action to KeptListManager.

components.name: ListMcpServer
components.encapsulates: Encapsulates Invocation-protocol volatility for MCP tools. Assistants invoke every list action; routes to KeptListManager.

components.name: KeptListManager
components.encapsulates: Encapsulates Change-propagation volatility and the list-action workflow. Sequences each action; announces kept changes.

components.name: ListRulingEngine
components.encapsulates: Encapsulates the list rules Presentation-host volatility must not copy: Title Check, Aggregate Done, View Selection, Tally.

components.name: TodoListAccess
components.encapsulates: Encapsulates Storage volatility. Atomic verbs over the kept Todo List: record, retrieve, revise, discard.

components.name: CallerAccess
components.encapsulates: Encapsulates Caller-identity volatility. Resolves a caller to the kept list it may act on.

components.name: TodoStore
components.encapsulates: Durable store for the kept Todo List. Survives app close, device and service restarts.

components.name: IdentityProvider
components.encapsulates: The team's identity provider. Verifies caller credentials.

components.name: MessageBus
components.encapsulates: Pub/sub messaging utility. Carries ListChanged to open views.

verdicts.summary:
Overall the decomposition is sound for a small system: one Manager behind four Clients (one per host and one per protocol), one Engine, two ResourceAccess components using business verbs, closed layering throughout, and a dynamic view for each of the 14 committed use cases. Checks pass. Three defects block approval. All three are fixed by changing the model's claims and drawing. None of them needs a reshaped use case.

BLOCKING

1. ListRulingEngine claims a volatility from the wrong layer (layer fit / no double claims). Its `encapsulatesVolatilities` is ["Presentation-host volatility"]. That volatility is about where and inside what the list is shown, and how people act on it. It is a Client-layer volatility, and WebApp and McpAppsSurface already own it as its two host facets. The Engine does not contain host change. It holds the rules that the volatility's EFFECT clause says must not be copied into hosts. Citing the volatility whose damage you are avoiding is not encapsulating it. Every rule the Engine carries is explicitly REJECTED in the committed .volatilities: Title Check is variableNotVolatile, Aggregate Done and View Selection are natureOfTheBusiness, and the Remaining Tally is variableNotVolatile. As drawn, the Engine joins to a volatility it does not hide, and a third claimant appears on Presentation-host with no ratified facet group. Fix it one of two ways. (a) Fold the fixed list rules into KeptListManager's own work and remove the Engine. With 1 Manager and 0 Engines the golden-ratio rule is not breached for a system this size. (b) Keep the Engine, but give it an honest disposition: escalate a volatility amendment, or record a conscious waiver on the draft for an Engine that hides no committed volatility. Do not cite Presentation-host volatility. Whichever you choose, the Engine's `encapsulates` prose and typed list must agree.

2. Change-propagation volatility has no receiving seam (trigger honesty / delivery obligation). KeptListManager publishes ListChanged to message-bus. But no relationship anywhere carries ListChanged back to an open view: no Client subscribes to message-bus, and no edge goes from message-bus to a Client. Review Where the List Stands, node x3, says a view "re-runs whenever an open view is told the list changed elsewhere". So the model claims a re-trigger it cannot structurally cause. The volatility's own rationale ("Likely an operational-concept disposition (pub/sub)") also points out that the volatile part, the delivery mechanism (re-read, polling, push, host notification), does not live inside the Manager's publish call. Fix: (a) draw the subscribe edges from each UI-surface Client (WebApp, McpAppsSurface) to message-bus. A Client may call a Utility, and this is that Client's own business work, not ambient. (b) Record on the draft an explicit operational-concept deferral for the delivery mechanism, to be resolved in .operationalConcepts. (c) State what KeptListManager itself contains, which is what is announced and when. Its `encapsulates` prose then tells the truth about where the Change-propagation volatility is split.

3. Caller resolution is drawn in some views and silently missing from views of identical work (cross-Manager symmetry / realization truth). resolveCaller → caller-access → identity-provider is drawn in these views: Work the Kept List, Review Where the List Stands, Assistant drives the list, Come back and find the list, and View and work embedded. It is missing from Capture a todo, Reword a todo, Remove a todo, Mark a todo done or remaining, Mark all todos, Clear finished todos, Switch between views, and See how many todos are left. In those views KeptListManager calls retrieveList(listRef) or discardTodos on a list it never resolved. KeptListManager always resolves the caller; that is the Caller-identity seam. Eight realizations therefore show the same entry work at a coarser grain and misstate what captureTodo/removeTodo/etc. do. Fix: in each of those eight views, add the resolveCaller → caller-access → identity-provider pair to the entry-node fragment, right after the Client → KeptListManager call. This is the same pattern Work the Kept List already uses at n1. No activity node changes.

NON-BLOCKING (record or fix at your discretion)

- TodoListAccess.reviseTodos carries three different business acts: retitle one todo, set one todo's done state, and set every todo's done state. That is an update-shaped verb behind a glossary name. I accept record/retrieve/revise/discard as the ratified Keep List vocabulary. Consider whether retitle and mark-done-state should be separate atomic verbs.
- Recount granularity varies. Capture, Reword, Remove, and Mark re-read the list (retrieveList) before TallyRemaining. Mark All and Work the Kept List (n6) tally the todos they already hold. Both are valid, but pick one idiom so that comparable steps are drawn at the same grain.
- Clear finished todos picks out finished todos with SelectView(completed). The core view does the same thing with DecideChange. Reusing a rule is fine, but name it the same way in both views.
- Engine operations are PascalCase (CheckTitle), while Manager and ResourceAccess operations are camelCase. This is cosmetic.
- Sharing Invocation-protocol across ListApi/ListMcpServer and Presentation-host across WebApp/McpAppsSurface is accepted: each pair is one Client facet per host or protocol.

verdicts.summary:
1) [Blocking: scope defect] "Team" says "the small group of people who share and work one todo list", and "Todo List" says "the ordered collection of the team's todos". Both make one shared multi-user list part of the domain. The sources disagree. The behavior contract says "the app manages a list of todos for a single user/session" and lists "multi-user sharing" as explicitly out of scope ("must not be assumed required"). The founder brief speaks of each person's own list ("add it to their list", "people losing their todos"). "For our team to try out" names who will trial the app. It does not ask for a shared list. As written, this glossary would pass multi-user sharing on as a requirement into volatilities, use cases and design. Fix: reword Team as the group trialling the app. Make the list belong to one user (Team Member). Reword Todo List, Keep List, Record Todo and Discard Todos ("the team's kept list") to match. Automated Assistant should then work that same user's list, not "the team's" list.
2) [Minor, fix while you are there] "Keep List" uses "a user", which no term defines. Use "Team Member" (or whatever the owning party becomes after fix 1).
3) [Non-blocking, taste] Consider saying what Mark All Done does on an empty list (nothing to do). The source does not cover this, so leaving it out is acceptable.
Everything else is accurate and complete against the contract. That includes blank-title handling, reword-to-blank removing the todo, abandoning a reword, the toggle-all rule for mixed and all-done lists, Clear Finished doing nothing when nothing is finished, view selection never changing todos, a remaining count independent of the view, and backend persistence that survives service restarts.

The abstraction is sound and I accept it from the customer side. Two cores: changing the list and seeing where it stands. Six customer-named mutations collapse under Work the Kept List and four read-side asks collapse under Review Where the List Stands. Every nonCore entry has a rejection reason and a variationOf that resolves to a core. The two channel-shaped asks (assistant through agent tooling, embedded MCP host) are correctly rejected as Invocation-protocol and Presentation-host permutations. All five drafted volatilities are crossed by the core flows. Lanes are business areas (Caller / Todo List / Other Open Views), which fits Pass-1 doctrine. What needs fixing:

1) [Blocking: realizable actions, retrieve-then-select pair] Review Where the List Stands, n2 "Retrieve the kept list's todos in order…" followed by n3 "Select the todos belonging to the chosen view and tally the remaining…". This is the retrieve-then-select padding shape. One read returns the chosen view's todos, so an honest realization leaves one of the pair with no call (CC-COVERAGE). Fix: collapse them into ONE fresh-select action, e.g. "Retrieve, in order, the kept todos in the chosen view together with the items-left count across the whole list". Keep the tally as its own action only if you can name the separate component call that computes it. Apply the same fix to the nonCore "See how many todos are left" (n1 retrieve → n2 tally). Keep the user-visible outcome note x2 as it is.

2) [Blocking: realizable action] Abandon a rewording, n1 "Discard the in-progress wording in the host and show the todo's kept title again". By your own rejection reason this never reaches the kept list. It re-renders a title an earlier read already produced, and no component makes a new call. Reclassify it as a note and keep the outcome ("the todo keeps its original title; nothing on the kept list changes"). Do NOT delete the entry or the behavior: customers expect Escape to abandon an edit. If the schema demands at least one action node, record why this host-local gesture has none rather than inventing a call.

3) [Blocking: scope wording, carries the open glossary defect forward] Work the Kept List's essenceRationale says "Changing the team's kept list" and "make the change visible to everyone else working the list". Multi-user sharing is out of scope in the behavior contract, my glossary critique flagged exactly this, and your own volatilities draft rejects List-sharing volatility. Reword so the list belongs to the Team Member, and so the "others" who must see a change are that member's other open views and the Automated Assistants working the same member's list. Not other people. Fix the same phrasing in Review Where the List Stands ("the list is kept on the team's behalf"). Keeping it on the team's behalf rather than on the device is fine; sharing it among teammates is not.

Non-blocking (taste, fix if convenient):
- The Clear finished todos rejection reason says it is "the same flow without a recount", but the core flow always recounts (n6 on the fork). Either drop the clause or make the recount conditional in the core flow. A recount that never changes is harmless.
- Note that mission, glossary and volatilities are still drafts, not committed, on this branch (the glossary has an open revise). This critique was made against those drafts. If the glossary rework renames the owning party, re-check the actor names here.

message-bus.content:
# MessageBus: Requirements / Scope Note

Activity: C-message-bus (Build MessageBus, 10 days, junior-developer, risk bucket 2). Layer: **Utility**. Contract key: `messageBus`.

## 1. What this component is

The committed System calls it a "Pub/sub messaging utility" that "carries ListChanged to open views". It is a Utility, not a business component. It holds no list rules and no storage. It does not decide anything about todos. It is the transport that the Manager uses to announce that a kept list has changed.

It is how the design carries out the **Change-propagation volatility**. That volatility belongs to KeptListManager: the Manager decides *that* a change is announced and *when*. MessageBus provides the *mechanism* that delivers the announcement, so the Manager does not depend on how the announcement reaches others (polling, server push, host-delivered notification). The volatility entry itself predicts this: "Likely an operational-concept disposition (pub/sub) rather than its own component."

## 2. Responsibilities (each traced to the committed design)

| # | Responsibility | Trace |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | Accept a `ListChanged` announcement from KeptListManager after a list action has been kept. | Relationship `kept-list-manager → message-bus` (sync, `publish(ListChanged)`). |
| R2 | Make that announcement available to the open views of the same kept list, so that a change made by one actor (a Team Member through a host, or an Automated Assistant through agent tooling) reaches the open views of other actors. | Component description "Carries ListChanged to open views". Change-propagation volatility. Mission objectives 4 and 6. |
| R3 | Do this the same way for every changing action. Publication is the last step of every changing use case. | Dynamic views: work-the-kept-list n7, capture-a-todo n3, reword-a-todo n5, remove-a-todo n3, mark-a-todo-done-or-remaining n3, mark-all-todos-done-or-all-remaining n5, clear-finished-todos n3, assistant-drives-the-list-through-agent-tooling n3. |
| R4 | Receive nothing on read-only paths. | Dynamic views that make no call to message-bus: review-where-the-list-stands, abandon-a-rewording, switch-between-all-active-and-completed-views, see-how-many-todos-are-left, come-back-and-find-the-list-as-it-was, view-and-work-the-list-embedded-in-an-mcp-host. |

MessageBus makes **no outbound calls** in the committed System. It calls no Engine, ResourceAccess or Resource, and that must remain true. A Utility does not reach into business layers.

## 3. Callers / consumers

- **Publisher (modelled):** KeptListManager is the only caller in the committed design. It calls synchronously, once per changing action, after the change is kept (after TodoListAccess has written and, in the general flow, after TallyRemaining).
- **Subscribers (described, not modelled):** "open views". By the volatility text, these are the open views of a Team Member in the WebApp or the McpAppsSurface. No subscribe/deliver edge from message-bus to any client appears in the relationships or the dynamic views. See open question Q1.
- **Not callers:** Engines, ResourceAccess and Resources. Clients publish nothing; every change goes through KeptListManager.

## 4. Non-functional constraints

**Maintainability**
- Keep it business-agnostic. The bus carries a `ListChanged` notice and does not interpret todos, titles, done state or counts. Business meaning stays in KeptListManager and ListRulingEngine.
- It must be small enough for a junior developer to build and test in one 10-day activity. Do not gold-plate it: no general-purpose broker features (routing DSLs, replay, durable queues) unless Q2 requires them.

**Extensibility**
- The delivery mechanism is the volatile part (re-read, polling, server push, host notifications). Changing or adding a mechanism must not change KeptListManager's call.
- Adding a new presentation host or protocol must not require changing the publisher.

**Security**
- Scope announcements to one list. A `ListChanged` for one kept list must reach only the open views entitled to that list. Caller-to-list resolution is owned by CallerAccess (Caller-identity volatility), and the bus must not undo it by broadcasting across lists.
- Notices carry no more than they need. They must not be a side channel that leaks todo content to views not entitled to it.
- The bus does not authenticate callers itself. Identity is resolved upstream by KeptListManager → CallerAccess.

**Reliability / correctness**
- The record of truth is the kept list, not the bus. A `ListChanged` that is lost or late must never lose a recorded todo, because the change is already durable before publish (mission: "No recorded todo is ever lost").
- The edge is sync. The Manager's action must not be held hostage to slow or absent subscribers. Whether a publish failure fails the list action is open question Q3.
- The contract requires the remaining count to be the true count, refreshed after every changing action. The bus is what lets this hold across actors: after an announcement, an open view must be able to reach the truth again (by re-reading through the normal review path).

## 5. Out of scope

- Deciding what changed, or computing views or tallies (ListRulingEngine).
- Storing todos (TodoListAccess / TodoStore).
- Resolving identity (CallerAccess / IdentityProvider).
- Multi-user list sharing, offline sync, undo/history, analytics or logging feeds. These are all rejected volatilities.

## 6. Open questions for Detailed Design

- **Q1 Subscriber side not modelled.** The System says "carries ListChanged to open views", but no message-bus → client (or client → message-bus subscribe) edge exists in relationships or dynamic views. Detailed Design must decide how an open view registers interest and receives notices, and whether this needs an upstream System amendment rather than invented scope.
- **Q2 Operational concepts not committed.** `operationalConcepts` (the sync/queued and pub/sub disposition, infra building blocks) is not yet committed on this branch. The delivery primitive, the ordering and delivery guarantees (at-most-once vs at-least-once), and whether notices persist must follow that disposition, or the platform runtime doctrine, once available.
- **Q3 Publish failure semantics.** On the sync `publish(ListChanged)` edge, does a bus failure fail the list action, or is it logged and swallowed because the change is already kept? This affects the Manager's error handling.
- **Q4 Notice payload.** What does `ListChanged` carry: just the list reference, or also the action kind or remaining count? The minimum is preferred under the security constraint. It must be confirmed with KeptListManager's contract.
- **Q5 List scoping key.** Which list reference (from CallerAccess's resolution) scopes subscriptions, and how is entitlement to subscribe checked?
- **Q6 Self-notification.** Should the acting view receive its own `ListChanged`? This is harmless if views re-read, but it affects test expectations.

## 7. Test-planning notes (scope, not design)

The test client needs to: publish from a stand-in for KeptListManager; observe delivery to one or more stand-in open views of the same list; prove there is no delivery to another list's views; prove publish behaviour with no subscribers; and confirm that a failed or absent delivery never affects the already-kept list.
